title: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
summary: Formally deprecates TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1, which lack support for current cryptographic algorithms and which many industry and government profiles now forbid. The documents that defined them, RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, are moved to Historic status. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Two old versions of the lock that protects web traffic have been retired because newer locks are much safer.

questions: what tls version is the minimum now
subtitle: The IETF formally retires TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0 and says implementations must not negotiate them.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 lack current cryptographic algorithms, depend on SHA-1, and keep older, riskier options alive in products and libraries.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8996 moves the TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0 specifications to Historic and says TLS 1.0 and 1.1 MUST NOT be used or negotiated, with a minimum of TLS 1.2 (DTLS 1.2) in the RFCs it updates.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers must not offer or accept these versions. A peer that receives such a Hello must answer with a protocol_version alert and close the connection.

today: RFC 8996 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 195) and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 5469 and RFC 7507, and it moved TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 to Historic.

sections.title: What the RFC Deprecates
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346) were superseded by TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) in 2008, and TLS 1.2 has itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446). Datagram TLS (DTLS) 1.0 (RFC 4347) was superseded by DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) in 2012.

RFC 8996 therefore deprecates TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0, and the documents that defined them have been moved to Historic status. It does not deprecate DTLS 1.2, and there is no DTLS 1.1. The goal is to give developers extra justification to drop old versions and migrate to a minimum of (D)TLS 1.2.
sections.eli5: Some old editions of a rule book have been taken off the shelf. Everyone is asked to use the newer editions from now on.

sections.title: Why the Old Versions Have to Go
sections.content:
The RFC lists several technical reasons. The old versions require older cipher suites that are no longer desirable; for example, TLS 1.0 makes TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement. They do not support current recommended cipher suites, especially authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers, which were not supported before TLS 1.2.

Handshake integrity and peer authentication both depend on SHA-1. Supporting four TLS protocol versions also raises the chance of misconfiguration, and the RFC notes that at least one widely used library planned to drop TLS 1.0 and 1.1, which would push products to keep running older library versions.

The RFC adds that mitigations exist for the currently known vulnerabilities, but future issues in old versions might not be fixed in older libraries once newer libraries stop supporting those versions. It quotes NIST's account of how TLS 1.1 fixed weaknesses in TLS 1.0 around initialization vectors and padding errors, TLS 1.2 added SHA-2 and AEAD cipher suites, and TLS 1.3 introduced a new handshake and key derivation.
sections.eli5: The old locks use weak parts that clever people have learned to pick, and the shops that make locks are stopping production of them, so it is safer to switch.

sections.title: The SHA-1 Problem
sections.content:
Both TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 rely on a running SHA-1 hash of the exchanged messages to protect the handshake. This makes it possible for an attacker able to perform 2^77 operations to mount a downgrade attack on the handshake, which is well below the acceptable modern security margin.

Authentication of the handshake uses signatures made with a SHA-1 hash, or a concatenation of MD5 and SHA-1 hashes that is not appreciably stronger. An attacker able to break the weakened hash could impersonate a server.

Neither version lets the peers select a stronger hash for signatures in the ServerKeyExchange or CertificateVerify messages. The only upgrade path is therefore a newer protocol version.
sections.eli5: The old versions check that nobody tampered with the conversation using a stamp that is now too easy to forge. They cannot switch to a better stamp, so the only fix is a newer version.

sections.title: The Rules: TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 MUST NOT Be Used
sections.content:
For both versions the rule is the same: the version MUST NOT be used, and negotiating it from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted. In practice, clients MUST NOT send a ClientHello with client_version set to {03,01} (TLS 1.0) or {03,02} (TLS 1.1), and servers MUST NOT send a ServerHello with server_version set to those values.

Any party that receives a Hello message with the protocol version set to {03,01} or {03,02} MUST respond with a protocol_version alert message and close the connection.

There is one interoperability allowance. Specifications were never clear about what the record layer version number (TLSPlaintext.version) may contain in a ClientHello, and RFC 5246 Appendix E allows it to be chosen for interoperability. So TLS servers MUST accept any value {03,XX} (including {03,00}) as the record layer version for a ClientHello, but MUST NOT negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: do not start a conversation using the old lock, and if someone offers it, say no and hang up. You may still read the label on the envelope, but you must not use the old lock.

sections.title: Updates to Other RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 8996 updates a long list of RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or DTLS 1.0. The update obsoletes use of the older versions and prohibits fallback to them. Mandatory minimum versions of TLS 1.0 or 1.1 become TLS 1.2, and a minimum of DTLS 1.0 becomes DTLS 1.2. Statements that TLS 1.0 is the most widely deployed version and gives the broadest interoperability are removed without replacement.

It also updates RFC 7525 (BCP 195, the TLS best-practice document). Sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 of that RFC change SHOULD NOT to MUST NOT for negotiating TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0. This is why RFC 8996 is itself part of BCP 195. It likewise updates RFC 6347, which had allowed negotiating DTLS 1.0.

Two documents are obsoleted. RFC 5469 (DES and IDEA cipher suites) is moved to Historic because the only TLS versions that defined them are now Historic. RFC 7507 (the fallback signaling cipher suite value) is marked Obsolete, since TLS 1.3 detects downgrade through sentinel values in ServerHello.Random.
sections.eli5: Many other rule books said "use the old lock at least". This RFC goes through them and changes that to "use the newer lock at least".

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
TLS 1.1 has been obsolete since RFC 5246 in 2008, and DTLS 1.0 since RFC 6347 in 2012. Some systems in operation may still not support (D)TLS 1.2 or higher. Following this RFC when talking to them will cause a failure to interoperate.

Ignoring the recommendations to keep interoperating carries some risk. The RFC points to its Sections 2 and 3 for the nature of those risks and says they should be weighed, together with any mitigating factors and the risks of updating the systems in question, when deciding how quickly to adopt the recommendations.
sections.eli5: A few very old gadgets may not understand the new lock. Talking to them the safe way will not work, so owners must decide how fast to upgrade them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document deprecates two older TLS versions and one older DTLS version for the security reasons already described. Its security argument is that the attack surface is reduced when fewer protocols are supported and fallback options are removed.

The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Fewer doors means fewer doors for a burglar to try, so closing the old ones makes the house safer.

items.label: TLS 1.0
items.desc: Must not appear in client_version or server_version; a receiver answers with a protocol_version alert and closes the connection.

items.label: TLS 1.1
items.desc: Must not appear in client_version or server_version; a receiver answers with a protocol_version alert and closes the connection.

items.label: Record layer version
items.desc: Servers must accept any value, including {03,00}, in the record layer version of a ClientHello, but must not negotiate TLS 1.0 or 1.1.
